7. The economics of obesity: a research agenda
This section proposes a research agenda for the economics of obesity.
7.1. Obesity measurement

An important priority that relates to every aspect of research on this subject is the need for social science datasets to collect higherquality data: measurements rather than self-reports of weight and height, plus more accurate measures of fatness (Burkhauser and Cawley, 2009). Ideally, this would include body composition – fat and lean mass – measured by state-of-the-art technology (the NHANES currently uses Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry), and would include information not just on quantity of fat mass but also its location in the body. Even measured waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio, though less accurate, would be of value because they reflect central adiposity.

In addition to more accurately measuring fatness, social science datasets could facilitate research on this subject by collecting genetic data (which can be analyzed for genetic predispositions to obesity and risky behaviors generally). Blood tests for diabetes and high cholesterol would provide other objective data that relates to fatness and diet. Time diaries would help researchers determine the amount of time people spend in recreational exercise as well as food preparation and eating, and sedentary activities like commuting or television watching; the most detailed time diaries are available in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS), and they are also available in the Child Development Supplements (CDS) of the Panel Survey of Income Dynamics (PSID). Such time diaries should collect information on eating as a secondary activity (as in the ATUS’s Eating and Health Modules of 2006–2008) because much eating today takes place at the same time as other activities, such as watching TV and driving (see, e.g. Hamermesh, 2010).

Several social science datasets have taken the lead in collecting higher-quality data.17 The National Longitudinal Survey of Adolescent Health (Add Health) has repeatedly measured respondents’ weight, height, waist circumference, and in addition analyzed genetic samples to provide information about genetic predispositions to risky behaviors. The three Early Childhood Longitudinal Surveys (ECLS-B, ECLS-K, ECLS-2011) include repeated measurements of weight and height. The Health and Retirement Study has, in its later waves, measured weight, height, waist circumference, analyzed blood spots for cholesterol, tested for diabetes, and collected genetic information. The PSID’s CDS contains measurements of weight and height for youth (but not adult respondents to the main survey).

However, nearly 15 years after the National Research Council published a report on the importance of biomarkers for understanding the association of socioeconomic status with health and mortality (NRC, 2001), several social science datasets continue to collect no more than self-reported weight and height. The Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) contains self-reported weight and height, and self-reported historic diagnosis of diabetes, which is a particular challenge for estimating the health care costs of obesity or diabetes. The National Longitudinal Surveys of Youth (NLSY-1979, NLSY-1997) continue to collect only self-reported weight and height. Evaluations of obesity prevention and treatment programs should also collect a wide range of accurate and objective measures of weight and body composition; this is particularly important because interventions that make people more physically active may increase muscle while decreasing fat, so examining only BMI could obscure the benefits of the program.
7.2. Causes of obesity

The previous research on certain economic causes of obesity (e.g. education and the macroeconomy) has found mixed results. To some extent, the heterogeneous and contradictory findings may be due to differences in data and the subgroups among whom the Local Average Treatment Effect is measured. Future research should seek to resolve these discrepancies and estimate effects for subgroups of particular interest, such as children and the economically vulnerable.

Given the limitations of existing data, it may not be particularly fruitful or useful to estimate the percent of the historic increase in obesity that was due to a specific factor. Reversing the epidemic of obesity does not require reversing the original causes of that rise. Some of the factors that have been implicated in the rise in obesity, such as reduced smoking (Chou et al., 2004), technological change (Cutler et al., 2003; Bleich et al., 2008; Lakdawalla and Philipson, 2009; Philipson and Posner, 2003) and increased maternal employment (Anderson et al., 2003), may be socially desirable and we may not wish to reverse them.

To clarify, it absolutely is a priority to better understand the factors that contribute to obesity today. Economic research with good identification strategies often is unable to reject the null hypothesis of no effect from many possible causes, such as food prices, the time cost of acquiring food, income, and education. If these are not major contributors to obesity, it begs the important question: what is? Are the causes so multifactorial, person-specific or idiosyncratic that few factors will explain much variation for the population as a whole?

For certain possible contributors to obesity, such as income, food prices, and peers, randomized controlled experiments have provided valuable information. Conducting further randomized field experiments is a high priority. Clearly, they are most useful when they shed light on novel contributors to obesity, but even if they examine the same possible contributors, they can still provide important information because experiments tend to be conducted with relatively small, unrepresentative samples, and thus additional ones can shed light on robustness and generalizability.

Field experiments are of course expensive in time and money, and for some interesting questions cannot be conducted, and thus it will always be important to identify and exploit natural experiments. Again, studies of new causes and consequences are important, but even additional studies of the same contributors can be valuable because natural experiments tend to affect certain subpopulations, and it can is useful to gather information about many Local Average Treatment Effects.
7.3. Genetic markers

Genes are a particularly interesting natural experiment that epidemiologists refer to as Mendellian Randomization (Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2005). Genes are an appealing source of variation because they are beyond the individual’s control and long precede the outcome – they are determined even before birth. However, to date it has proven challenging to use individual genes as instruments for obesity (Cawley et al., 2011). They tend not to be powerful instruments because, although genetic factors play an important role in obesity (Farooqi and O’Rahilly, 2007; Pietilainen, 2014) individual genes tend to have little independent influence on weight and geneticists’ understanding of those processes are far from complete; all known genetic polymorphisms combined explain less than $2 \%$ of the variance in obesity (Winter et al., 2013). There have also been challenges to validity; some studies have used as instruments alleles that, in addition to being only very weakly correlated with obesity, are associated with other risky behaviors and thus are likely to affect the outcome through channels other than obesity (see the discussion in Cawley et al., 2011). One of the strongest papers in this area is Von Hinke Kessler Scholder et al. (2012), which instruments for fat mass using the genetic marker FTO, which is highly correlated with fatness and does not seem to have the problems with validity that plagued genetic instruments used in earlier studies. As genetic research on obesity progresses, the suitability of specific genes as instruments in specific circumstances should become clearer.

7.4. Obesity and risky behaviors

Another important direction for future research is to better investigate the extent to which the causes and consequences of obesity are similar to those for risky behaviors such as heavy or binge drinking, use of narcotics, abuse of prescription drugs, smoking, and unprotected sex. All involve dramatic tradeoffs between immediate gratification and future health, and thus rates of time discount and the extent of risk aversion are relevant (Cawley and Ruhm, 2012). For each, time-inconsistent preferences could have a substantial impact on behavior, and there is a potential conflict between the deliberative prefrontal cortex and the impulsive limbic system (Ibid). If risky behaviors had the same causes, one would expect to see a high correlation between them, but Cutler and Glaeser (2005) find that correlations across risky behaviors (both participation and changes in participation) tend to be below $1 0 \%$ . Most studies of risky behaviors tend to focus on just one or a few of them, and the field would benefit from research testing for similarities and differences between a large number of risky behaviors.

There are interesting research questions regarding the interactions of obesity with other risky behaviors. For example: are risky behaviors substitutes? Perhaps individuals can get their dopamine fix from a wide range of risky behaviors, but tend to become addicted to one and then not participate in others. There is considerable evidence that smoking suppresses the appetite; several studies find that youths, especially teenage girls, smoke in part to reduce their weight (e.g. Cawley et al., forthcoming; Rees and Sabia, 2010; Cawley et al., 2004).

It would also be interesting to know whether individuals who are quitting one risky behavior are at higher risk of initiating another. If so, can one manage this constructively to replace a harmful addiction like overeating with a beneficial one like exercise? Is there a life cycle progression of addictions: smoking in teenage years, heavy or binge drinking in the college years, overeating in adult years?
7.5. Consequences of obesity

Most of the causal estimates of the consequences of obesity are based on the use of the weight of a biological relative as an instrument; future research should seek to identify additional natural experiments for weight. One could also exploit randomized controlled trials of weight loss interventions to examine the effect of weight loss on economic outcomes, although samples may be small and the estimates may reflect not only the effect of weight loss but also that of the method of achieving it (e.g. bariatric surgery may temporarily affect productivity and exercise programs may have direct health benefits).

It would be useful to estimate the extent to which the wage penalty associated with obesity is the result of lower productivity or discrimination in the labor market. Studies of military recruits have documented worse job performance among those with excess weight (e.g. see the review in Cawley and Maclean, 2012) but there is little evidence on the causal effect of weight on productivity. There is also a need for estimates of the causal effect of obesity on other labor market outcomes, such as job absenteeism.

It would be a substantial contribution to more accurately calculate the external costs of obesity. To date, research has assumed that the external costs of obesity are substantial because: (1) medical care costs rise significantly at high levels of BMI; (2) premiums in group health insurance are not based on BMI, nor are the tax contributions to public health insurance based on BMI. Knowing the magnitude of these external costs would be useful when tailoring policies designed to internalize them through health insurance premia, taxes on items like energy-dense foods, or incentives for weight loss by the obese. Models for such an analysis are Sloan et al. (2004), which calculated the external costs of smoking, and Manning et al. (1991), which estimated the external costs of heavy drinking, smoking, and sedentary lifestyles.
7.6. Effective interventions

An important contribution can be made by evaluating the effectiveness of policies and interventions that seek to prevent or reduce obesity, and then using that information to improve them. The ACA of 2010 alone enacted several new programs: the nationwide menu labeling law, increased flexibility for workplace wellness programs to offer financial rewards for weight loss, awards to states to provide incentives for healthy behavior among beneficiaries of Medicaid and Medicare, and community transformation grants to promote healthier lifestyles.

Randomized controlled experiments involving programs related to obesity would be ideal. However, a simple and inexpensive thing that policymakers can do to improve our understanding of the effects of policies is to create more natural experiments. For example, some states, facing high Medicaid bills for treating obesity-related illness, have requested that the U.S. Department of Agriculture grant them a waiver to exclude energy-dense, low-nutrient foods from the SNAP program; SNAP could be made more like the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program, which provides a very specific set of foods selected by nutritionists and physicians (Institute of Medicine, 2006). However, to date the USDA has denied all such requests for waivers. Granting these waivers and allowing states to revise the terms of food assistance programs would create variation that could be used by researchers (after correcting for policy endogeneity) to identify effects of such programs.

Some challenges are philosophical. Neoclassical welfare economics assumes that each individual has a single utility function, but if the dual-process model of decision-making as described in Loewenstein and O’Donoghue (2004) and Ruhm (2012) is correct, then it is unclear “whose” utility should count: that of the farsighted and deliberative prefrontal cortex or that of the myopic and impulsive limbic system? Economists tend to seek to empower the prefrontal cortex, but does this put too little weight on the utility of the limbic system? Although some, including the former commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration (Kessler, 2012) have criticized industry for developing foods that appeal to our genetic predisposition to crave fat, sugar, and salt, these items are by construction very enjoyable. Should welfare economics count some weighted value of the utility of the two systems?

Despite this philosophical ambiguity, I think it is important to find better ways of helping people overcome their timeinconsistent preferences or empower their rational prefrontal cortex to control their impulsive limbic system. Dieting and exercise require continual short-term sacrifice in exchange for long-term health benefits, and people seek ways to lock in a future pattern of healthy eating and active living. Economists have a comparative advantage in designing commitment devices, like forfeitable bonds, to facilitate that decision (see, e.g. Bryan et al., 2010). Economists can also help design incentives for weight loss, healthy diets, and physical activity to help offset the high up-front disutility of these activities, with the goal of increasing retention and adherence. Considerable research is needed to determine the optimal design of such incentives, in terms of the medium of the reward (monetary or in-kind), its format (fixed reward or lottery), the optimal timing and frequency of such rewards, and whether the optimal design of rewards is different for achieving the weight loss than for maintaining the weight loss.

Another important priority for evaluating policies and interventions is to study offsetting behaviors. Most commonly, researchers study the impact of a policy on a single behavior in a single setting. However, when a single price is changed, purchases of all products may change, and offsetting behaviors may nullify the beneficial main effects. For example, people may respond to a tax on certain energy dense foods by increasing their consumption of other, untaxed, energy-dense foods (Fletcher et al., 2010a, 2013; Chouinard et al., 2007). Thus, not just own-price elasticities, but also cross-price elasticities, are important. Another example is that increasing physical education requirements in elementary school leads girls to reduce participation in discretionary playground activities and increase time spent watching television, with no net effect on weight (Cawley et al., 2013). Such compensatory responses appear to be common in exercise interventions (King et al., 2007). It can be difficult to track such offsetting behaviors, because they may take place at other times of day, at other venues, and with respect to either calorie intake or expenditure. For example, removing soft drinks from school cafeterias could lead youths to consume more soft drinks at home or on the way to or from school, or could lead them to expend less energy on the playground or at home. Evaluations of policies and interventions should seek to measure such offsetting behaviors in order to provide a complete picture of the effects of policies.
7.7. Explaining disparities and heterogeneity in effects

Investigating differences among different population subgroups, and using that information to tailor policies to those subgroups, is another priority. One important unanswered question about obesity is: why does it vary so much by race and ethnicity? In the NHANES data for 2011–2012, the prevalence of obesity was $1 0 . 8 \%$ among Asian-Americans, $3 2 . 6 \%$ among non-Hispanic whites, $4 2 . 5 \%$ among Hispanics, and $4 7 . 8 \%$ among non-Hispanic blacks (Ogden et al., 2014). Some of this difference is due to the fact that BMI ignores differences in body composition, and as a result BMI understates obesity in Asian-Americans (Jih et al., 2014) and overstates it in African-Americans (Burkhauser and Cawley, 2008). Within most race/ethnic groups, the prevalence of obesity is similar for women and men, but this is not true for African-Americans, among whom the prevalence of obesity is much higher among women $( 5 6 . 6 \% )$ than men $( 3 7 . 1 \% )$ (Ogden et al., 2014). Explaining these large disparities represents an intriguing direction for future research.

The published research often finds gender differences in the causes and consequences of obesity; e.g. SNAP receipt increases obesity for women but not men (Meyerhoefer and Pylypchuk, 2008), weight lowers wages more for women than men in the U.S. (Cawley, 2004), and there are peer effects on weight for women but not men (Yakusheva et al., 2014). In addition, the socioeconomic gradient in obesity across education and income is much stronger for women than men in economically developed countries (Sassi, 2010).

Future research should further investigate the reasons for these subgroup differences; e.g. to what extent is the greater obesity wage penalty among women than men in the U.S. due to a differential impact of obesity on self-esteem or differential discrimination by employers? It would be useful to know whether those with the highest consumption of calories are less responsive to food taxes, perhaps because they have the strongest habits. If those who impose the greatest externalities are price inelastic, taxes would not change their behavior but could still be used to internalize external costs. It is also important to better understand whether consumer response to nutrition labels varies by educational level. If so, should the required nutrition label be that which is optimal for the less educated?
7.8. Behavioral economics approaches

The terms “behavioral economics” and “nudge” have been applied quite broadly, to include even very neoclassical approaches such as altering time costs, offering incentives, providing information, and harnessing peer effects. Clarity about which approaches are consistent with neoclassical economics and which are implied only by behavioral economics would be helpful.

Undoubtedly, future research will investigate the effect of various nudges to consumer behavior. Diet in particular seems to be a very promising area in which to apply this approach, because in supermarkets and cafeterias there is a clear, prominent, and potentially influential architecture of choices. In restaurants, menus have a choice architecture, and there are defaults that can be manipulated, such as portion sizes and included side orders.

It may not be realistic to expect that small changes in choice architecture (or prices or other incentives) will have large, lasting effects (Marteau et al., 2011). Diet and a sedentary lifestyle can be habitual or addictive behaviors (Linden, 2011) with stable steady states (Becker and Murphy, 1988). For consumers in a stable steady state, small changes have little or no lasting effect – people quickly go back to their old habits.18 This may explain why behavior changes tend to evaporate after incentives are removed; see e.g. John et al. (2011) and Just and Price (2013). Replication studies of nudges will be a high priority; it is important to determine which findings are robust and which effects are long-lasting.
7.9. Cost effectiveness analysis

Another important priority is to assess the cost-effectiveness of existing programs and policies. In order to achieve the greatest increase in social welfare from a given budget devoted to obesity prevention, money should be allocated to programs based on their cost effectiveness. Studies have calculated the cost-effectiveness of both surgical and pharmaceutical treatment of obesity (e.g. Michaud et al., 2012) as well as many prevention programs (see Lehnert et al., 2012; Roux, 2011, for reviews), but for many programs not only the cost-effectiveness but even the effectiveness is unknown. The ACE (Assessing Cost Effectiveness) Obesity America project seeks to use a consistent methodology to measure the cost effectiveness of a wide range of interventions, and builds on a similarly ambitious program conducted in Australia (see Carter et al., 2009). Given the number of candidate interventions to be evaluated, there remain many opportunities to conduct costeffectiveness analyses of obesity policies and interventions, and evaluations of new programs designed to treat or prevent obesity should include a CEA component.

8. Conclusion

The large literature on the economics of obesity indicates that numerous economic variables, such as food prices, the time cost of food acquisition, income, education, the macroeconomy, and peer behaviors, may have modest effects on weight and obesity. The magnitude, and sometimes the sign, of these effects vary by subgroup (e.g. gender, race, age, and income). There appears to be no single dominant economic cause of obesity; instead, a wide variety of factors may each contribute a small amount, and different economic variables may be relevant for different groups.

In contrast, the consequences of obesity are relatively clear: lower wages and higher medical care costs that impose negative externalities through health insurance. There exists an economic rationale for government intervention in order to internalize the negative externalities of obesity and provide information to consumers. Justifying government intervention on the grounds that consumers behave irrationally is contentious, and more widely accepted for children than adults.

Research on economic approaches to treatment and prevention suggests that providing additional information through menu labels, taxing energy-dense foods, and offering financial rewards for weight loss, while justifiable as methods of addressing market failure, may have only modest effects on weight. Thus, just as there is no single cause of obesity there is no magic bullet that will reduce obesity; instead, a wide range of policies may be needed to have a substantial effect on the prevalence of obesity. An important caveat is that considerable research remains to be done to determine ways of making information, taxes, and financial rewards more effective in changing behavior. The large number of important research questions that remain suggests that the economics of obesity will continue to be an active and fruitful research area for many years to come.

Abstract. I present new stylized facts on the market for managers over the twentieth century, utilizing a novel data set on managerial careers. From the 1930s to the mid-1970s, the level of executive pay, inequality among executives across and within firms, and mobility were low. These patterns have reversed since then. I document that an increase in the importance of general managerial human capital can account for this change. The level of general skills, measured by the type of education and occupational mobility of managers, correlate with higher pay and turnover. Other factors may have also contributed to these changes, but the labor market for managers has likely played an important role.

1. Introduction

The rapid rise in executive pay in the United States since the 1970s, particularly relative to the wages earned by other workers, has stimulated an extensive literature on executive compensation (Hall and Liebman 1998, Murphy 1999, Hall and Murphy 2003, Bebchuk and Fried 2003). Over this period, CEOs have also become increasingly mobile across firms (Huson et al. 2001). Surprisingly, the mobility and remuneration of top managers are often studied independently and, even when they are related, the workings of the labor market for executives receive little attention.1 This paper contributes new facts on the mobility, compensation, and careers of top executives over most of the twentieth century, with the aim of integrating the labor market to our understanding of the changes in pay and turnover. This long-run perspective suggests that an evolving market for corporate executives may have played an important role in the development of the compensation and mobility of top managers.

An understanding of the long-run trends in the market for corporate executives has been hampered by a lack of consistent data (see Bertrand 2009 for a critical review of the literature). Using hand-collected information on the compensation and the biographies of about 1,000 executives from 1936 to 2003, I find that the level of total compensation and managerial turnover have followed a J-shaped pattern over this period. The inequality among top executives, both across and within firms, was relatively stable until the 1970s, but it has increased rapidly since then.

The educational background and the experience of top managers have also evolved over time. I find that executives were more likely to obtain degrees in a technical discipline prior to the 1960s, but that formal education in business has become more common since then. Moreover, managers used to concentrate their expertise in one area (for example, rising to top leadership through various promotions in the sales sector exclusively) early in the twentieth century, but the diversity in their occupational experience has increased steadily over time. The changes in educational background and in occupational diversity are suggestive of a transformation in the types of managerial skills. I argue that the market for executives has increasingly placed more weight on general human capital, and less on firm-specific managerial skills. This shift may help to account for the changes in compensation and managerial mobility over the long run.

To illustrate that such a shift in the type of skills could lead to an increase in pay, inequality, and mobility, I present an equilibrium model of the labor market for executives based on Murphy and Zábojnik (2004), Murphy and Zábojnik (2007). As in their framework, managerial ability is comprised of firm-specific and general skills, but only the latter are transferable across firms. I depart from their setup by studying the compensation of not only CEOs but also of other top executives in a model with search frictions. These frictions impede perfect assortative matching between executives and firms and introduce a wedge between a manager's compensation and her productivity within the firm. Specifically, managerial pay depends on the manager's outside option, which is determined by the executive's productivity in new firms. This outside option increases with the generality of managerial skills.

In this framework, an increase in the importance of general skills leads to higher levels of compensation, higher turnover, and higher pay inequality. As general skills become more important, the manager's outside option increases, leading to higher equilibrium levels of executive pay. Turnover also rises for two reasons. First, higher levels of pay render low productivity firms unprofitable, which choose to stop operations. Second, high productivity firms endowed with low-ability managers choose to fire them because the benefit of hiring new managers on the job market is higher when those managers have higher levels of general skills. Finally, in the model the degree of skill generality determines the sensitivity of executive pay to managerial ability, but it also affects the endogenous allocation of talent across firms. In my setup, the first effect dominates; the distribution of executive pay both across all managers and among top managers within firms therefore widens with the increasing importance of general skills.

To assess the model's predictions, I use principal components to create an index of the generality of human capital based on the education and occupational experience of managers, and relate it to pay and mobility. The predictions of the theoretical framework are borne out in the data. A one-standard deviation in the index is associated with an $1 1 \%$ increase in the annual level of pay, a $7 \%$ increase in managerial mobility (measured by the number of firms an executive worked for during his career), and an $8 \%$ increase in income inequality across top executives within the firm relative to the mean.

Two important caveats should be taken into account when interpreting these magnitudes. First, the skill set of executives is obviously endogenous, and these estimates are therefore correlations. Understanding the determinants of the shift in observed managerial skills is important. Although a detailed analysis of the driving forces of such a shift exceeds the scope of the paper, several factors may have increased the demand for general managerial skills over the century. I discuss possible sources for this shift in Section 5.

Second, the change in the types of managerial skills has been small relative to the large increases in the level of pay, inequality, and mobility. From the late 1930s to the early 2000s, managerial turnover increased by about $3 8 \% ,$ within-firm inequality among top managers rose by $6 5 \%$ , and the average level of total compensation in the sample increased by a staggering $8 7 0 \%$ . Thus, while the implied elasticities of pay, turnover, and inequality with respect to skill generality obtained from the regression analysis are substantial, it is likely that other factors also contributed to the sharp changes in these trends over time.

This paper contributes to the large literature studying the determinants of executive compensation.² The importance of general managerial skills for the growth in CEO pay in recent years has been discussed both theoretically (Murphy and Zábojnik 2004, Murphy and Zábojnik 2007) and empirically (Custodio et al. 2013). I add to this literature by showing that a shift in the types of managerial skills may have contributed to the trends in compensation and in mobility over most of the twentieth century. Whether other countries have experienced a similar transformation is an interesting open question. Unfortunately, the United States is the only country to have required the disclosure of executive compensation in a systematic way for a long time period; instead, international comparisons are generally based on recent data (see, for example, Fernandes et al. 2013). Thus, this paper provides a unique longrun perspective on the market for corporate executives.

A growing literature finds that CEO characteristics affect a variety of firm policies and outcomes (see, for example, Bertrand and Schoar 2003, Malmandier et al. 2011, Schoar and Zuo 2016). The novel long-run trends in managerial careers that I put forth show that CEO characteristics have evolved greatly over time. An open question for future research is to study whether these new stylized facts have had consequences for firm outcomes over the twentieth century.

Executive compensation, turnover, and career paths are complex phenomena, and it is therefore unlikely that a single factor could account for the evolution of these measures over 70 years. In Section $5 ~ \mathrm { I }$ discuss other factors that have probably contributed to the long-run trends. However, the findings of this paper suggest that the labor market has played an important, but relatively ignored, role in this process.
2. Long-Run Trends in the Market for Managers

One of the main objectives of the paper is to establish the long-run trends in the market for managers, and to relate them to the changes in executive compensation over the twentieth century. This section provides a description of the data collection, briefly summarizes the long-run trends in compensation established by Frydman and Saks (2010), and presents new evidence on managerial careers.
2.1. Sample Selection

Constructing a consistent data set on the compensation and careers of executives over the twentieth century is challenging for several reasons. A first step requires identifying the names of top managers for a sizable number of firms. Commonly used data sets, such as Compustat's Executive Compensation database (ExecuComp), only provide this information for recent decades. I build on the work by Frydman and Saks (2010) who hand collect the names and remuneration of individual top executives for 101 large publicly traded U.S. corporations (corresponding to the 50 largest firms in 1940, 1960, and 1990) since the 1930s. Their sample is a good starting point for the purpose of this study because it allows me to track the compensation of individual executives over time.

A further challenge is to obtain information on managerial careers over a long time horizon. The Frydman-Saks sample provides the names of executives, but it lacks information on the characteristics of these individuals. I hand collect information on their educational background, demographic characteristics, and job histories from biographical sources. This data collection process is extremely time-consuming; thus, I focus on a subsample of the Frydman-Saks data: the three highest-paid executives in the 50 largest firms in 1960 (measured by the value of sales) from 1936 to 2003. Appendix Table B.1 provides a detailed list of these firms. Focusing on firms that were large in the 1960s leads to an unbalanced panel over time, but it allows to have a sizable number of firms that were large throughout most of the twentieth century.3 As discussed in Section 2.4, this balanced subsample is important to understand the trends in managerial mobility over the long run.

Executive pay exhibits similar patterns in the sample of the 50 largest firms in 1960 than in the full Frydman-Saks data, which is representative of the largest 300 publicly traded firms in the economy in any given year. The trends are also robust to restricting the sample to the 708 managers with available biographical information, the subsample that is used in the regression analysis in Section 4.
2.2. New Data on Managerial Biographies

A considerable literature in sociology and economics has studied the educational background, career paths, and social status of executives at different points in time. (See Friedman and Tedlow 2003 for a comprehensive review of this literature.) Because each study uses a different design and focuses on different aspects of managerial careers, they cannot provide a systematic understanding of the long-run evolution of the market for corporate officers. To construct a consistent, longrun panel data set following the careers of top executives within the same set of firms, I collect biographical information for the three highest-paid executives of the 50 largest firms in 1960.

For each individual who appears in the compensation data set from 1936 to 2003, I obtain information on education, age, career paths, and other personal characteristics from the printed versions of Who's Who in Industry and Commerce for various years and the Biography Resource Center from Gale Research.4 Although the Biography Resource Center usually contains information on the jobs of individuals after they left the firms included in my sample, I do not collect this information to be consistent with the data obtained from printed versions of Who's Who. Thus, my data exclude any job that the executive started after the last year in which he is observed in the compensation database. A detailed description of all the variables constructed from the biographical data is presented in Appendix A.

The initial sample of the three highest-paid officers contains 1,545 individuals, of which $6 3 \%$ are matched to biographical records. I restrict the sample to the 903 executives for which year of birth is known, since this information is necessary to compute various important variables. The likelihood of obtaining biographical information is higher for more recent decades, and for more important personalities. Consequently, the sample is skewed toward including more presidents and chairmen, but fewer vice presidents and other lower-ranked officers, relative to the initial compensation data set.5 The findings of this paper are therefore an accurate representation of career paths only for those executives who had successful careers in large corporations.

Biographical sources list each subsequent position held by the executive. For each job, I collect information on the name of the company, the year in which an executive started and ended a position, the job title, and (when available) the name of the division, sector of the firm, or specific function held by the officer. The reported career histories are not always complete. To avoid introducing biases because of missing information, I further restrict the sample to the 708 managers for whom a fairly "complete" work history (that is, since they entered the labor force until the last year in which they appear among the three highest-paid executives in the firm) is observed.6 The results are robust to using the full sample of 903 executives. Panel A of Table 1 provides basic descriptive statistics for both samples. To construct a consistent picture of the typical top executive in a given year, I match the biographical information to the panel data set on compensation. Thus, each executive appears in the sample for every year in which he was among the three highest-paid officers in the firm. The final data set contains a total of 4,900 person-year observations.

2.4.2. Mobility of Managers Across Corporations. The turnover of CEOs in publicly traded corporations has increased substantially since the 1970s (Murphy and Zábojnik 2007, Huson et al. 2001). This increase in mobility is more pronounced when external turnover occurring through takeover or bankruptcy is also considered (Kaplan and Minton 2012). While the recent trends in CEO turnover are well documented, little is known about mobility patterns over the longer run. Prior studies suggest that turnover may have actually decreased earlier in the twentieth century (Newcomer 1955), but the overall long-run trend is hard to assess because the mobility measures and sample definitions vary widely across these studies.

I provide a consistent description of the evolution of top management mobility over time. Because the companies in this study are among the largest in the economy (and thus have a larger internal labor market and may be less likely to change their recruiting policies), the documented mobility rates are probably lower than those in the average firm in the economy (as well as those reported in the studies cited previously).

Table 4 presents basic statistics on the evolution of managerial career paths since the 1930s. The average tenure of executives (measured as the number of years as an employee of the corporation in the compensation data set) gives a first indication of the changes in external mobility. The number of years worked at the firm increased from an average of 24 years in the late 1930s to almost 29 years in the 1960s.11 Average tenure began to decline in the 1970s, and by the 1990s it had recovered its prewar level. These changes are not a mere reflection of an increase in the duration of careers in the 1950s and 1960s. As shown in Table 4, it took the same number of years since entering the workforce for an executive to reach the very top of the corporate ladder (defined as being the president, chairman or vice chairman of the board, CEO, CFO, or COO of the parent company), or to become one of the three highest-paid executives in the corporation, throughout the entire time span of the sample. Thus, managers spent a larger fraction of their careers working at the same firm in the 1950s and 1960s than in recent years, and than in earlier decades.

To assess changes in mobility in more detail, I study the number of firms that executives worked for during their careers. Constructing this measure from biographical data is challenging because changes in the name of the company that an individual works for may represent different types of transitions. An executive may change firms in search of a better or different job, or because he is fired. Alternatively, executives may move across subsidiaries of a firm, or transition across firms because of takeovers.

To separately identify these cases, I construct two definitions of a firm and, consequently, two measures of mobility across companies. First, I consider an organization to be defined by the parent company, all subsidiaries, and all acquired companies.12 Following this broad definition of a firm, I measure mobility excluding moves of executives between subsidiary companies or because of mergers. I also construct a narrow measure of external mobility that takes into account moves between subsidiaries and those because of mergers. These two measures focus on different aspects of managerial turnover and help illuminate how careers have evolved over time. The broad definition highlights the poaching of executives by outside firms. Movements because of mergers or across subsidiaries may instead reflect changes in the skill composition of executives. Specifically, the decision to retain personnel of the acquired company following a merger may be influenced by the specificity of the employees' human capital. Movements across subsidiaries are more likely to occur in diversified firms operating in different markets. Thus, these movements may reflect a higher level of general skills or be part of a firm's strategy to increase the general human capital of its employees.

The trends in mobility described thus far may be biased because they are based on firms that were large in 1960. Unsuccessful firms may drop out in the later years of the sample, as they go bankrupt, merge into another company, or become privately held. This feature may lead to overstate the recent increase in mobility if executive turnover is lower in firms that are in decline. Moreover, mobility rates may be overstated in early decades in the sample because some companies were relatively new at that time, and thus necessarily hired employees with prior experience in other firms.

To address this concern, Figure 6 limits the sample to the 19 firms that appear in the compensation data set for every year from 1936 to 2003. The fraction of executives that spent their entire career at the same firm is higher for balanced panel of successful firms, but the mobility patterns remain roughly unchanged relative to Figure 5. The decline in mobility rates early in the twentieth century is less marked and more concentrated in the earlier years for the sample of 19 firms, suggesting that some of the decline in turnover in the overall sample was due to the maturing of firms. In contrast, the lack of mobility at midcentury, and the rise in turnover since the 1970s, are more pronounced in the balanced sample. On average, $7 0 \%$ of the executives in this balanced sample had not worked at another company from the 1940s to the 1960s, but less than half had worked exclusively at the same firm by the end of the sample (and only about $3 0 \%$ had done so when considering a narrow definition of the firm). This check confirms that top executive mobility has followed a J-shaped pattern over the twentieth century.

Even though mobility rates appear to have been high both early and late in the twentieth century, the underlying causes of managerial turnover may have been different in these two periods. Firms were significantly smaller during earlier decades, and thus the opportunity for upward mobility within a given organization was limited. The earlier part of the sample also contains several founders of companies, who usually worked for more than one corporation before becoming successful entrepreneurs. In contrast, the increase in outside hiring to replace outgoing CEOs during the past 30 years suggests that managers are now likely to switch firms late in their careers.

To provide suggestive evidence that the reasons for managerial mobility may have changed over time, I study differences in the timing of moves over the career path. This measure is also relevant because turnover may have different implications for the accumulation of managerial skills at different stages in the career. If moves occur early in the career, employees are still likely to acquire significant amounts of firmspecific human capital at their main employer. Instead, a move at the end of ones career suggests that firmspecific skills are less important. Table 6 shows the average age for the first and the last move for top executives that switched firms.13 For both measures, the average age upon a move was fairly constant from the 1930s to the 1960s, but it increased substantially since the 1970s. Conditional on moving, executives experienced their first and last moves when they were 10 years older by the end of the sample than those managers that switched firms earlier in the twentieth century. This difference is striking, since the average age of executives has remained remarkably stable over time.

2.4.3. Diversity of Occupational Experience. Biographical information also offers the opportunity to analyze changes in the occupational mobility of managers. 3. Theoretical Framework

The long-run trends presented in the previous section suggest that pay and managerial mobility have not changed in isolation, but rather have been accompanied by a substantial transformation in the characteristics and the careers of top managers. A plausible explanation for these patterns needs to match the following facts: the level of pay followed a J-shaped pattern, declining during the 1940s and increasing since the late 1970s; inequality among all top executives and within firms experienced a minor decline until the 1950s, and has increased rapidly since the 1980s; managerial turnover experienced a J-shaped pattern, declining until the 1950s and increasing since the 1970s, but the mobility in the earlier decades occurred when executives were young, whereas now managers are likely to switch firms fairly late in their careers; top managers used to have mostly technical or general education, but the fraction of executives with a formal education background in business has steadily increased since the 1960s; and the diversity in occupational experience has increased throughout most of the century.

A possible explanation for these trends is a shift in the types of skills over time, from firm-specific human capital to general managerial skills. Murphy and Zábojnik (2004), Murphy and Zábojnik (2007) show that this shift can lead to an increase in the level of pay (fact 1) and in turnover (fact 4). As I argue in more detail in Section 4, the shift toward business education (fact 5) and in the diversity of occupational experience (fact 6) are indicators that managerial human capital has indeed become more general over time. To also explore the relationship between skill generality and pay inequality across all managers (fact 2) and within firms (fact 3), I build a simple equilibrium model of executive pay in which firms have multiple managers. As in Murphy and Zábojnik (2004), Murphy and Zábojnik (2007), there is a distinction between firm-specific and general skills, but only general skills are transferable across firms. I depart from the Murphy and Zábojnik setup by introducing a search and matching friction that impedes perfect assortative matching across firms and managers and creates a wedge between a manager's marginal product and his wage.

The model shows that an increase in the relative importance of general human capital can lead to higher pay, higher inequality in executive pay, and more mobility of managers across firms. When managerial skills are mostly specific to the firm, firms are constrained to their initial executive pool, as hiring external candidates entails a substantial loss in productivity. In this case, managerial mobility is low because specific skills are not transferable across firms. The level and dispersion of compensation are therefore low, since the managers' outside option is both low and similar for all executives. As general human capital becomes increasingly valuable, the outside option of all executives increases, leading to higher equilibrium levels of pay. Managerial turnover increases as more productive firms endowed with low-ability managers benefit from poaching high-ability CEOs from less productive firms, and as more low-productivity firms shut down because the wage cost of executives is higher. Finally, the degree of skill generality determines the sensitivity of executive pay to managerial ability, as well as the allocation of talent across firms. The model predicts that the distribution of executive pay, both across all managers and among top managers within firms, widens as general skills become more important.

3.1. Setup

The general setup of the theoretical framework is as follows. The model has two periods, $t = [ 1 , 2 ]$ . In the first period $t = 1$ , productivity and skills are realized, and firms make their decisions. Specifically, at the beginning of the first period firms draw a random firm productivity level and managers draw a skill level; the best manager at the firm assumes the job of the CEO. At the middle of the period, existing firms decide whether to continue operations or exit the market. After the exit decisions are made, continuing firms make hiring decisions; firms can fire their existing managers and search for a replacement. At the beginning of the second period $t = 2$ the managerial labor market clears. Exiting firms are potentially replaced by new firms. Output is realized and wages are paid.

3.1.1. Firms and Managers. There is a continuum of existing firms indexed by $k \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . At the beginning of period 1, each firm draws a productivity level $\theta \sim$ $U [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Although I loosely refer to $\theta$ as the firm's productivity level, in reality this parameter captures a variety of factors that influence the sensitivity of firm outcomes to CEO ability. The productivity draw is observable.

Each firm has two managerial job positions, $j = [ 1 , 2 ]$ . I term these positions as the CEO $( j = 1 )$ and the division head $( j = 2 )$ . Firms need to fill both positions in order to operate, and they enter the period with two (randomly allocated) managers. Managers are heterogeneous in terms of skill $\alpha _ { i }$ At the beginning of the first period, each manager draws an independent draw $\alpha _ { i } \sim$ $U [ 0 , 1 ]$ Themanaer with the highe abilit w, $\alpha _ { 1 }$ is assigned to the CEO job. The manager with the lowest ability draw, $\alpha _ { 2 }$ becomes the firm's division manager. In what follows, I assume that both $\alpha _ { 1 }$ and $\alpha _ { 2 }$ are observable.

Importantly, skills are imperfectly transferable across firms. A fraction $\xi$ of a manager's skill is general, while the remaining fraction $1 - \xi$ is firm specific. General skills are transferable across firms, whereas firmspecific skills are only valuable at the firm where they were acquired. The parameter $\xi$ determines the relative importance of general versus specific skills. For simplicity, I abstract from the formation of firm-specific skills. One possibility would be to consider that the internal managers being considered for the CEO and division manager jobs had spent some time at the firm acquiring these skills.

3.1.2. Firm Exit. After observing their productivity level and their initial allocation of managers, firms decide whether to continue operations or to exit the market. If a firm exits the market, its managers become unemployed and look for a job in the managerial labor market.

3.1.3. Hiring Decisions. Continuing firms make hiring decisions. Firms make "take it or leave it" offers to their current managers. That is, I assume that existing firms have all the bargaining power. In addition, they decide whether to fire their existing managers (or equivalently offer them a wage that they know will be refused), and whether to post a job opening to fill the job of a manager who is fired. There are no costs associated with posting a vacancy.

3.1.4. The Managerial Labor Market. Managers searching for a job have two options. First, they can search for a job in one of the existing firms. Their second option is to start a new firm. These two alternatives are nonexclusive: starting a new firm is always possible. Hence, unemployed managers might as well search on the job market; if they are unlucky, or if they get a wage offer below their reservation threshold, they always have the option of starting a new firm.

The labor market for managers is subject to a search and matching friction. Specifically, a manager searching for a job will be randomly matched to a firm that posts a vacancy. Let $M _ { u }$ be the measure of managers looking for a job, and $M _ { v }$ be the measure of job postings by existing firms. Then, the probability that a manager is matched to a firm that is looking to hire is defined by

$$
\lambda = \operatorname* { m i n } \left( \frac { M _ { v } } { M _ { u } } , 1 \right) .
$$
Managers that enter the labor market and are not matched to any of the existing firms are randomly matched in pairs, and they have the opportunity to start new firms.

3.1.5. New Firms. Creating a new firm requires at least one manager. All new firms formed by unemployed managers start at the same productivity level $\theta _ { N } \in$ [0, 1].14 Here, I allow for the possibility that the productivity of new firms is different than the mean productivity of existing firms; if the two are the same, then $\theta _ { N } = 1 / \overset { \triangledown } { 2 }$ .

Creating a new firm with two managers requires no additional resources. If the new firm is created by only one manager, an additional cost $c$ is required. This cost c can reflect, for example, the additional overhead costs associated with running a firm without a division manager, or the cost of hiring and training a fresh graduate. If both managers cooperate, each manager obtains a payoff equal to her Shapley value.
3.1.6. Production. At $t = 2$ uncertainty is realized and output is produced. A manager $i$ who was initially matched to, and is currently employed by firm $k$ ,produces a flow of output equal to

$$
q _ { i k } = b + \theta _ { k } \alpha _ { i } ,
$$

as long as she stays in the firm where she started her career. That is, a manager output has two components: a fixed amount $b$ regardless of her skill level, and a component that is multiplicative in her ability and the firm's productivity level. The constant $b$ captures the component of CEO productivity that is independent of ability, for instance, managerial effort.
If the manager moves to firm $k ^ { \prime }$ , part of her skill set is no longer valuable; in a new firm $k ^ { \prime }$ she produces

$$
q _ { i k ^ { \prime } } = b + \xi \theta _ { k ^ { \prime } } \alpha _ { i } .
$$
3.2. Equilibrium

I begin the analysis by first deriving the equilibrium wage for a manager of ability $\alpha _ { i }$ . The manager always has the option to start a new firm at productivity level $\theta _ { N }$ . Her expected payoff from doing so is equal to

$$
\bar { w } _ { i } = b + \alpha _ { i } \xi \theta _ { N } .
$$
Since existing firms have all the bargaining power, they will always offer a wage that is exactly equal to the manager's outside option (4), implying that $w _ { i } = \bar { w } _ { i }$ .

In equilibrium, the wages of all managers are given by (4). Managers in existing firms receive their outside option, which is given by (4). The same will be true for new firms. Specifically, since $c > 0$ and the firm's output is equal to the sum of the output of its respective managers, newly created firms will always start with two managers. Each manager will receive (4), which equals her Shapley value, or equivalently, her marginal contribution to the firm.15 Hence, executive compensation in this model depends on the productivity of new firms, as, for example, in Eisfeldt and Papanikolaou (2013).

A manager searching for a job will be matched to an existing firm with probability $\lambda$ . Instead, with probability $1 - \lambda$ the manager will exercise the option of starting a new firm. Since the manager's expected payoff is the same in either case, the manager's expected payoff from searching is independent of $\lambda$ .

Since only general skills are transferable across firms, the fraction of skill generality $\xi$ determines the sensitivity of the manager's equilibrium wage to ability. Thus, the level of executive pay is increasing in $\xi$ (fact 1). In this case, managers on the job market are indifferent between getting a job in an existing firm or starting their own firm. Hence, their expected payoff from going on the job market is independent of the likelihood of finding a job $\lambda$ , and it is therefore also equal to (4).

Next, I examine the model's predictions about turnover. Consider an existing firm with productivity $\theta _ { k }$ . The firm decides first whether to continue operating or to shut down. The firm's profits, defined as output minus wage costs, are equal to

$$
\Pi _ { k } = \sum _ { j = 1 , 2 } ( q _ { j k } - \bar { w } _ { j } ) = ( \theta _ { k } - \xi \theta _ { N } ) \sum _ { j = 1 , 2 } \alpha _ { j } .
$$

Equation (5) implies that firms whose productivity level is too low $( \theta _ { k } \le \xi \theta _ { N } )$ will be unprofitable no matter the skills of the managers they employ. These firms will exit the market and their managers will be without a job. The measure of the firms that exit the market is equal to $\xi \theta _ { N }$ . Since each firm employs two managers, there will be at least $2 \xi \theta _ { N }$ managers looking for a job. This implies that there will always be more unemployed managers than firms posting vacancies, so searching firms are always guaranteed to find a match.

Now consider a firm that is sufficiently productive $( \theta _ { k } \ge \xi \theta _ { N } )$ and decides to continue its operations. If the firm were to instead replace the manager in position $j$ with a new hire $i$ from outside the firm, the profits that the firm would generate from that manager would be equal to

$$

$$
Since the matching of executives to firms is random, the expected payoff to firm $k$ from searching for a manager is equal to

$$
\Pi _ { k } ^ { \prime } = ( \theta _ { k } - \theta _ { N } ) \xi \bar { \alpha } ,
$$

where $\bar { \alpha }$ denotes the average ability level of managers on the job market. That is, the firm expects to hire a manager of ability level $\bar { \alpha }$ , who will have no skills specific to firm $k$ and would therefore produce $b + \xi \theta _ { k } \bar { \alpha }$ .In equilibrium, the firm expects to compensate this manager by $b + \xi \theta _ { N } \bar { \alpha }$ .

In sum, the model delivers predictions that are consistent with the stylized facts that I document in Section 2. Specifically, an increase in the level of generality of skills leads to (1) higher levels of executive pay, (2) increase in pay inequality across all top managers in the economy, (3) increase in pay disparities among top managers within firms, and (4) increase in managerial turnover. In deriving these predictions, I have made several simplifying assumptions. The assumption that is most important for tractability is that the matching between executives and firms is initially random. Since firms can also fire their low-ability managers, the model can be interpreted as a model of assortative matching with search frictions. Allowing firms to search for executives with a particular level of talent is a potentially interesting extension, and one that would likely resemble more closely the actual labor market for top corporate executives. In that case, I would expect to see a stronger pattern of assortative matching than in my model.
4. Empirical Evidence: Skills, Pay, and Mobility

According to the model, the long-run trends in pay, inequality, and turnover may reflect the growing importance of general managerial skills over time. But has such a change in skills actually occurred? Changes in the types of formal education are suggestive of such a transformation: MBA degrees probably confer general knowledge that is useful for different industries, whereas degrees in engineering and science may be more valuable in specific industries. The increased diversity in occupational experience also seems consistent with a shift toward general managerial human capital. Individuals with general skills are arguably more likely to work successfully in different sectors.

Moreover, firms may rotate executives through different sectors of the firm to provide general skills or to assess whether individuals would be successful at leading a diversified and complex organization.

Although these trends are suggestive, they do not establish a correlation between skills, turnover, and compensation. To better grasp this relationship, I use principal components to construct an index of the generality of managerial skills based on education and occupational experience, and relate the variation in this index to pay and mobility.

It is important to note that education and occupational experience are plausible proxies for the generality of managerial skills that do not require a change in the importance of those skills ex ante. In related work, Custodio et al. (2013) build on the methodology developed in this paper to create a similar index of general managerial skills using modern data. In contrast to my strategy, their measure of general ability is mostly based on the mobility of executives across firms and industries. This measure is potentially problematic because, according to theoretical models, the turnover of executives across firms (and therefore across industries) is a direct outcome of the importance of general skills. Thus, in my main analysis I do not utilize these measures to proxy for the types of skills.17
4.1. An Index of the Generality of Human Capital

I define two indicator variables for whether a manager's latest educational degree achieved was "technical" or "business." These variables are not mutually exclusive because a substantial fraction of the executives had neither technical nor business education. The omitted category contains "other types of education," defined as general degrees (such as BA or MA degrees with no specified major), and degrees in other nontechnical and nonbusiness fields (such as law and medicine, among others).

Using principal components, I combine the variables for technical and business education with the measure of occupational mobility to construct a unidimensional index of general human capital at the manager level. Appendix B, Table B.2 reports the loadings on all three factors. Only the first principal component has an eigenvalue above one and it alone explains about $5 0 \%$ of the variation. Moreover, this factor can be interpreted as a measure of general skills, as it loads positively on the measure of occupational mobility and on business education, and negatively on technical education. Thus, I build the index based on this factor. I interpret high values for the index as indicative that a higher fraction of a manager's skills are general. The index is standardized to have a mean of zero and standard deviation of one.

5. Interpretation of the Findings

The analysis thus far takes a shift in the importance of general managerial skills as given, but investments in formal education, individuals' willingness to accumulate experience in various sectors, and firms' decisions to provide certain skills on the job are endogenous choices. Still, these choices may be an optimal response to an exogenous change in the weight of general skills in the firms' production function. A resulting question is the following: Which factors could have caused such a change in the type of skills over time?

One set of explanations involves advances in technology. Recent decades saw an increase in the complexity and scale of firms caused by the rise in general purpose technologies, such as information technology, and advances in analytical methods for decision making. These changes have been used to explain the increase in the returns to skills over time for a variety of occupations (Goldin and Katz 2008).

In addition, American businesses experienced transformations that may have had a more direct impact on the skills of top management. First, firms became increasingly industrially and geographically diversified, which may have resulted in higher demand for general managerial skills. The market value of firms responded positively to conglomerate diversification of the 1960s and 1970s (Baker 1992, Hubbard and Palia 1999, Klein 2001), and to geographic diversification (Bodnar et al. 1997). Companies may have benefited more from these undertakings when their top officers had skills general enough to successfully manage corporation spanning different industries, countries, and cultures. 23

Although large firms are still diversified geographically, they have become increasingly specialized since the 1980s, and the average diversification premium is now negative (Morck et al. 1990). But at the same time, the top hierarchy of firms has become flatter (Rajan and Wulf 2006). Improvements in communication and information technology now allow a larger number of employees to report directly to the CEO and other top managers (Garicano 2000). The ability to process diverse information and make decisions that affect various divisions of the firm may have increased the value of general skills at the top of the organization (see Bertrand 2009, for further discussion).
5.1. Mechanisms Affecting the Relative Importance of General and Specific Skills

An extensive literature debates the causes for the recent rise in executive pay, but most of the proposed explanations are silent on turnover and managerial careers. A challenge for any theory is to account for all of the long-run stylized facts established in this paper. The two most popular explanations view compensation as either the result of the competitive assignment of CEOs to firms, or the outcome of rent extraction by powerful CEOs (Jenter and Frydman 2010). Interestingly, these theories have implicitly opposite views on the workings of the labor market. Next, I consider each in more detail.

Prompted by the recent works by Tervio (2008) and Gabaix and Landier (2008), the view that compensation is the outcome of an optimal assignment of talented CEOs to firms has gained a lot of attention. These models predict that the level of pay should increase over time with the size of the typical firm. The longrun trends in executive pay present a challenge for this explanation because the size of firms increased rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s, a period in which the growth in executive pay was almost negligible (Frydman and Saks 2010). But the shift in the type of managerial skills may actually provide a way to accommodate this theory with the time-series evidence. The definition of talent in these models is akin to general skills. Allowing for talent to be composed both by general and firmspecific skills introduces a friction in the labor market. Thus, executive pay may have remained relatively low at midcentury even if firms were expanding rapidly, provided that managerial talent was largely firm specific. It is more difficult to determine the prediction of these models for the trends in turnover.24 In their most strip-down form, these models present a frictionless the labor market where executives never move (if the ordinal ranking of firms does not change), or where they move immediately in response to any change in the size ordering of firms.

The opposing view of compensation argues that managerial pay is the inefficient result of rent extraction by powerful CEOs (Bebchuk and Fried 2003). A priori, this theory has little to say about turnover. It is possible, however, to argue that CEOs would choose to move across firms when corporate governance is weaker if they extract rents mainly by negotiating a new contract. For example, Khurana (2011) claims that the labor market for CEOs has large frictions that allow external candidates to extract rents from coopted boards. Still, the managerial power hypothesis cannot explain why the education background and the occupational experience of top managers evolved over time.

In sharp contrast to the managerial power hypothesis, an improvement in corporate governance may actually offer a complementary explanation to the general skill hypothesis put forth in this paper. Hermalin (2005) shows theoretically that improvements in boards' ability to monitor executives may increase the threat of separation, which in turn could result in higher turnover and compensation. Although Hermalin does not explicitly model the skill accumulation process, it is intuitive to think that managers would choose to invest more in general skills when the threat of working for multiple firms over their career is higher.25 Empirically, the rise in institutional investors over time may have actually strengthened the ability (and incentives) of boards to monitor CEOs. Thus, the increased importance of general managerial human capital could be the endogenous response to an exogenous improvement in the corporate governance of firms.

It is of course impossible to determine whether the importance of general managerial skills in the firms' production function, the corporate governance of firms, or both, have changed exogenously over time. However, qualitative evidence suggests that the shift in managerial skills is a plausible explanation for the documented changes in executives' education. For example, a survey administered to 300 CEOs in the late 1960s found that executives with educational backgrounds in engineering and physical sciences thought that a formal education in finance and business would have provided them with better preparation for their job as CEOs (Stieglitz 1969). Another indication of the transformation in the skills of managers was the expansion of executive development programs in universities, which began in the late 1950s. Corporations sent their top executives back to school because top managerial jobs were becoming more complex, and because executives' skills needed to be upgraded as organizational practices and managerial decision making become increasingly scientific (West and Sheriff 1969).
5.2. Alternative Explanations

This paper establishes a series of stylized facts on managerial careers over most of the twentieth century. In combination with the long-run trends in executive pay documented by Frydman and Saks (2010), these facts provide a challenge for the most common explanations for the recent rise in compensation. I propose that the long-run trends in the level of managerial pay, inequality among managers, and the external mobility of corporate officers can be partly explained by a shift in the importance of general managerial skills. Following Murphy and Zábojnik (2004), Murphy and Zábojnik (2007), I present a simple framework to show that an increase in the importance of general skills can lead to higher levels of pay, higher levels of managerial turnover, and more inequality among top managers.

Two main pieces of evidence are suggestive of the rising importance of general managerial skills over time. First, the type of formal education of top executives changed significantly, from managers having mostly a technical background early in the century, to most executives investing in general business education in recent years. The diversity of occupational experience has also steadily increased over time. I find that executives with higher general human capital received on average higher compensation and were more likely to switch companies. Also, disparities in pay among top managers within the firm were higher when the highestpaid executive had more general human capital.

While the increase in the generality of managerial skills was steady throughout the century, executive pay and mobility evolved in a J-shaped pattern. The growth in executive pay, the inequality among managers, and turnover was particularly pronounced since the mid-1970s. Hence, the timing of the effects suggests that other forces interacted with the documented changes in the labor market to give rise to the soaring levels of pay in the past three decades. Among other factors, changes in social norms and improvements in board monitoring may have contributed to the acceleration in absolute and relative CEO pay witnessed in recent decades. Yet, the interaction of compensation, turnover, and characteristics of managers documented in this paper suggest that changes in the labor market for corporate executives may have played an important role.

In 1980, Zimbabwe rapidly expanded access to secondary schools, providing a natural experiment to estimate the impact of increased maternal secondary education on child mortality. Exploiting age specific exposure to these reforms, we find that children born to mothers most likely to have benefited from the policies were about $2 1 \%$ less likely to die than children born to slightly older mothers. We also find that increased education leads to delayed age at marriage, sexual debut, and first birth and that increased education leads to better economic opportunities for women. We find little evidence supporting other channels through which increased education might affect child mortality. Expanding access to secondary schools may greatly accelerate declines in child mortality in the developing world today.

1. Introduction

Across the world, studies have generally found that more educated people live longer and healthier lives, and they give birth to fewer but healthier children (Grossman, 2006). However, only a few of these studies have been able to identify causal evidence of the impact of education, and very few studies have been conducted in the developing world (Lochner, 2011). In addition, very few studies have been able to investigate mechanisms through which improved education might affect health outcomes. Given the disproportionate share of the burden of disease as well as persistently high child mortality and fertility rates in developing countries, there is a need to better understand what role education might play in improving development outcomes today.

The major challenge to better understanding these relationships has been identifying situations in which education has increased in a way that is unrelated to other factors that might also affect health. The most successful studies have looked at natural experiments, usually changes in compulsory schooling laws or age-at-entry policies, to identify plausibly exogenous changes in education. Generally, most of these studies have found that increased levels of education are associated with lower (own) mortality, improved healthy behaviors (including smoking), lower fertility, and lower child mortality; however, not all of the studies come to the same conclusions1. Although evidence is sparse, there is also some evidence that educating mothers might lead to different outcomes than educating fathers, and that higher levels of schooling may be more important than primary schooling (Lochner, 2011).

In 1980, following independence, Zimbabwe rapidly expanded access to secondary schools for black Zimbabweans, which provides an opportunity to estimate the impact of increased maternal secondary education on child health and fertility outcomes in a setting with both high child mortality and high fertility2. Using age-specific exposure to a set of policies that greatly increased secondary school opportunities for some women, we first estimate the impact of increased maternal education on child survival3. The magnitude of our main result is large: children born to mothers who attended some secondary schooling are 12 percentage points less likely to die, and an additional year of schooling decreases the probability of a child dying by about $2 1 \%$ . We find that the effects are much stronger in rural areas and among less wealthy mothers.
