Closely related to our work are some recent U.S. studies that attempt to estimate the effects of the introduction of Medicare Part D on drug utilization.2 Almost all of these studies suggest large utilization effects on prescription drugs but the magnitudes vary considerably. For the elderly, Medicare Part D has been found to increase monthly drug use by 5.9 to 27 percent (Yin et al., 2008; Lichtenberg and Sun, 2007; Liu et al., 2011; Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010) or 11 to 37 percent among the previously uninsured (Kaestner and Khan, 2012; Schneeweiss et al., 2009) or to increase drug spending by 74 percent among the previously uninsured (Zhang et al., 2009). A few studies of the Part D transition period find no utilization effects. For example, Basu et al. (2010) find no significant changes in number of prescriptions because of Medicare Part D for Medicare–Medicaid dual eligible beneficiaries.

Optimal drug insurance design should also take into account how changes in drug coverage affect non-drug health service utilization. Such spillover effects in the broader context of free to patient physician and hospital services have received less attention in the Canadian pharmacare policy discussion. In contrast to the large literature on drug utilization effects, only a few studies have investigated the spillover effects of drug insurance on physician services with mixed findings. Some evidence suggests a complementary relationship between physician services and prescription drugs (Stabile, 2001; Allin and Hurley, 2009; Winkelmann, 2004) while other evidence points to a substitutive one (Li et al., 2007). A study by Kaestner and Khan (2012) finds no evidence that drug insurance was strongly associated with use of outpatient services. The RAND HIE, which is more than 30 years old, did not find evidence of cross effects of outpatient cost sharing on inpatient services. However, patients did not have free access to physician services in the HIE. Some existing studies also demonstrate that higher cost-sharing or a copayment for prescription drugs is associated with greater use of inpatient and emergency medical services (Tamblyn et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2006; Chandra et al., 2010; Afendulis et al., 2011). Tamblyn et al. (2001) find that emergency department visit rates increased by 14.2 per 10,000 person-months for the elderly persons after cost-sharing for prescription drugs was increased. Chandra et al. (2010) examine changes in copayments of prescription drugs and physician office visits for employees in the California public employees retirement system. They find significant “offset” effects in terms of increased hospital utilization in response to the higher copayments for prescriptions drugs and physician office visits. Afendulis et al. (2011) compare changes in the probability of hospitalization before and after the introduction of Part D in 2006 using a difference-in-difference-in-differences approach. They find that Part D reduced the hospitalization rate by 4.1 percent or 20.5 admissions per 10,000. However, other Medicare Part D studies do not find such offset effects on hospitalization (e.g., Liu et al., 2011; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). If we consider emergency department visits and hospitalizations as proxies for health, the studies reviewed above indicate that evidence on the health impact of prescription drug coverage is mixed and inconclusive.

Finally, comparatively few studies have examined the effects of prescription drug insurance on health status and functioning.3 If drug insurance causes an increase in drug and non-drug service utilization, the health impact depends on whether the increase in utilization is for effective high-value services to the patient. The existing literature on the link between drug insurance/cost sharing and health shows higher cost sharing is associated with more adverse events among the chronically ill, however, evidence on general health outcomes is rather limited (Goldman et al., 2007). The recently proposed Value-Based Insurance Design advocates that copayment rates be set based on the expected health value of the clinical services, so as to mitigate the adverse health consequences associated with cost-sharing for services or drugs (e.g., Fendrick and Chernew, 2006). By reducing patient copayments for high-value services, the value-based insurance plans can achieve improved health outcomes for a given level of health care expenditure. The current evidence suggests that reducing copayments can improve medication compliance among the chronically ill (e.g., Maciejewski et al., 2010). This line of literature also explores the effects of VBID programs on drug spending, nondrug medical spending, total spending and health service utilization (Chernew et al., 2010; Gibson et al., 2011; Choudhry et al., 2012; Nair et al., 2010). Chernew et al. (2010) find evidence that the VBID program reduced the use of nondrug health care services and offset the costs associated with increased drug use by the program. Gibson et al. (2011) find that the combination of VBID and disease management program resulted in sustained improvements in the use of medications and modest cost savings. Nair et al. (2010) examine the impact of reducing the prescription drug co-pay for diabetes and find that the policy was associated with decreases in emergency room visits, hospitalizations, physician visits and health care expenditures. In our context, if the mandatory drug program increases access to effective prescription drugs or physician services of high value to the beneficiaries, it may generate positive health gains. On the other hand, if the increased drug or physician utilization is not an effective treatment, it may not have any health impact.

In summary, many studies find consistent positive effects of drug coverage on drug utilization but the forms and magnitudes of cost sharing (e.g., copayments, coinsurance, caps and formulary restrictions) in these studies vary considerably as do the estimates. It is unclear whether these studies can inform the policy debate over a national pharmacare program in the Canadian context. Randomized experiments usually have small sample sizes and are not sometimes easily generalized to the population. Similarly, many Medicare Part D studies use data for a specific insurance plan, pharmacy chain or subgroup Medicare population. (Some exceptions include, e.g., Afendulis et al. (2011) and Kaestner et al. (2014)). These study samples and settings lack external validity and may not generalize to the rest of the population, although some of them advantageously use natural experiment research designs. In addition, enrolment in Medicare Part D is not mandatory while our study focuses on a policy design that enforces mandatory insurance coverage through legislation. Finally, to our knowledge, there are no studies that have examined the impact of drug insurance on health status in different parts of the health outcome distribution.
3. The institutional setting

Canada has a predominantly publicly financed health care system with 13 provincial and territorial health insurance plans operating under a national legislative framework. The Canada Health Act (1984) established five principles that the provincial health insurance plans must respect: public administration, universality, portability, comprehensiveness and accessibility. All provinces and territories provide universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services that are free at the point of use. The majority of public funding comes from general tax revenues of federal and provincial governments. Most hospitals are private, notfor-profit organizations funded through global budget. Physicians receive payments from provincial governments. The majority of physicians are remunerated by fee for service although new alternative payment models have been introduced in the past decade.

The late 1980s to early 1990s saw dramatic downsizing and restructuring in the hospital sector due to the government budget cutbacks. Hospitals were closed or consolidated into larger units. Caps and individual physician income threshold were imposed on physician expenditure in all or some provinces. All provinces except Ontario moved toward some form of regionalized governance for health care (Marchildon et al., 2006; Marchildon, 2004b). From late 1990s to early 2000s public health spending rebounded and provincial governments began to pour money back into health care. The 2003 First Ministers’ accord on health care renewal agreed on the priority areas for reforms: primary health care, home care, catastrophic drug coverage, access to diagnostic/medical equipment and information technology and an electronic health record. However, there has been little changes in the primary care sector at the system level until the early 2000s (Hutchison et al., 2001, 2011).

Outpatient prescription drugs in Canada are covered by a mix of public and private plans, in contrast to free publicly covered physician and hospital services. The federal government administers prescription drug programs for six specific population groups.4 Provincial and territorial governments provide public drug insurance to defined population subgroups, mainly for social assistance recipients, senior citizens, and residents with specific diseases that require high-cost prescription drugs.5 Eligibility and cost sharing arrangements in these public plans vary across provinces, and there have been some moves to decrease out-of-pocket payment in the past decade (Daw and Morgan, 2012).

Drug insurance coverage for the general population, i.e., the non-elderly not on social assistance, varies across provinces. Approximately 90 percent of those with private insurance obtain it through group plans associated with their employer, union or professional association (Hurley and Guindon, 2008). Public drug programs for the general population also exist in some provinces, but with high deductibles they only provide protection against catastrophic drug expenses.6 During the period of our study there were minimal changes of drug insurance policies for the general population in provinces other than Quebec.

Drug insurance in Quebec before 1997 reflected these general patterns: the public drug program covered welfare recipients, citizens aged 65 and over, and patients with certain serious illnesses. The public plan fully covered drug costs for low-income seniors and all welfare recipients; medium- and high-income seniors were subject to a $\$ 2$ copayment per prescription up to a maximum of $\$ 100$ per year. There was no public coverage for the rest of the population, who relied on private insurance or paying out-of-pocket. The Act Respecting Prescription Drug Insurance was passed in 1996 and went into effect in two stages (Gazette Officielle Du Quebec, 1996). The policy reform started with increased user fees for previously insured welfare recipients and senior citizens in August 1996. The mandatory universal drug program for every resident in Quebec was implemented on 1 January 1997. Under this program, all residents of Quebec were required by law to have drug insurance coverage. The public prescription drug insurance plan, administered by the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ), covers all Quebecers who are not eligible for a private plan. All persons under age 65 eligible for a private plan are required to join that plan and ensure coverage for their spouse and children.7 Private plans are usually available through employment or through membership in professional associations and unions. Coverage varies across private plans but all private insurers are required to provide minimum coverage standards that are equivalent to those offered by the provincial public plan. Persons who are eligible for a private plan cannot be covered by the public plan. The public plan charges an income-dependent premium that is collected by the Ministère du Revenu du Québec (now known as Revenu Québec) through the income tax system. In addition, the public plan includes a monthly deductible and coinsurance payment. Currently, the annual premium of the public plan varies from $\$ 0$ to $\$ 579$ depending on net family income, the monthly deductible is $\$ 16.25$ , and the coinsurance is 32 percent up to a maximum out-of-pocket expenditure per month of $\$ 82.66$ .
4. Data and descriptive statistics
4.1. Data

The main data set for this analysis is the master files of the longitudinal household component of the National Population Health Survey (NPHS), a biennial nationally representative survey conducted by Statistics Canada. The target population of the NPHS includes community-based household residents in the 10 provinces, excluding populations on Indian Reserves, Canadian Forces Bases and some remote areas in Quebec and Ontario. The sample was created by first selecting households and then within each household, choosing one member 12 years of age or older to be the longitudinal respondent. It also includes 2,022 persons who were under the age of 12 in the first cycle and previously interviewed as part of the 1994/1995 National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY).8 Therefore, the NPHS longitudinal sample includes 17,276 persons from all ages in 1994/1995. The NPHS asks a series of questions related to health status, use of health services, chronic conditions and activity restrictions, and demographic and socio-economic status.

We use the 1994/1995, 1996/1997, 1998/1999, 2000/2001 and 2002/2003 cycles of NPHS for our analysis. Of the 17,276 people who were first interviewed in 1994/1995, we excluded 2,022 people who were younger than 12 years old because most of the outcome variables are only available for respondents aged 12 and older. We dropped 4,086 people older than 56 in the first cycle. This resulted in a sample of 11,168 people aged 12 to 56 in 1994/1995, who were followed for up to eight years. The data were then re-shaped as person-year data containing 55,840 observations (11,168 times five cycles). We further deleted 3,824 observations reporting welfare benefits as their income source in any of the survey cycles. We then eliminated individuals missing important health care utilization information.9 The final data set consists of an unbalanced, non-contiguous panel of 10,653 people (42,609 person-year observations), who were non-elderly not on social assistance and between the ages of 12 and 56 in 1994/1995 (20 to 64 at their last interview in 2002/2003).

There are several reasons why we exclude from our analysis the elderly and social assistance recipients who had full drug coverage before 1996.10 First, the policy change for these groups happened at a different time, August 1, 1996, which is several months earlier than the reform for the non-elderly. Second, the reform had different implications for this previously covered group: it increased user fees for them (in contrast to providing drug coverage to the non-elderly). 4.2. Outcome variables

Drug insurance status is an indicator variable coded as one if a person reported having drug insurance and zero otherwise. Measures of health care utilization include drug utilization, physician visits and hospitalization. Drug utilization measures the number of distinct medications taken in the previous month.11 Note that this measure refers to both prescription and non-prescription drugs. Ideally we would separate these two, but separate measures are not available in the pre-policy cycles of the data. If the policy induces individuals to substitute prescription drugs for non-prescription drugs, our estimates would measure the net effects on total medication use and underestimate the impact of the policy on prescription drug use. Self-reported measures of medication use may introduce bias and measurement error.12 Therefore, we further look at aggregate drug expenditure from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) to complement our analysis. We measure general practitioner (GP) visits and specialist visits separately as the number of visits with each type of physician in the previous 12 months. Finally, all of the medication and physician utilization variables were truncated at their 99.5 percentile to eliminate outliers.13 For all utilization measures, we further look at the extensive margin of utilization: whether a respondent had at least one medication or physician visit. Hospitalization measures whether a respondent had an overnight inpatient hospital stay in the previous 12 months.

Health outcome measures are the health utility index (HUI3) and self-assessed health status. The Health Utility Index Mark 3 (HUI3) is a generic measure of health status and health-related quality of life that is widely used in clinical studies, population health surveys and economic evaluations (Horsman et al., 2003). It is a function of eight attributes that can vary from no impairment to severely impaired: vision, hearing, speech, mobility, dexterity, feelings, cognition and pain. For the HUI, 1.0 represents perfect health and 0.0 represents death. The observed values range from $- 0 . 3 6 0$ to 1.000 in increments of 0.001 (negative scores reflect health states considered worse than death) (Furlong et al., 1999). 4.3. Descriptive statistics

Figs. 1–3 depict trends in prescription drug coverage and medication utilization among the general population aged 12 to 64 in Quebec compared to the rest of Canada. The corresponding 95 percent confidence intervals are presented for all series whenever applicable. Fig. 1 shows that there was an increase in self-reported prescription drug insurance coverage in all provinces from 1996 to 2003. It is apparent, however, that Quebec started with a lower baseline level of coverage than the other provinces, and that right after the 1997 reform it experienced a dramatic increase in coverage from 62 percent to 85 percent. Interestingly, the magnitude of the increase in overage is very similar to that from the Medicare Part D studies. For example, Afendulis et al. (2011) find that Part D drug coverage increased from 61 percent in 2005 to 88 percent in

2007. Insurance coverage in Quebec continued to rise in the years after the policy change, reaching 93 percent in 2002/2003. The less than 100 percent coverage is possibly due to bias in self-reported insurance status, gaps between public and private plans, or failure to register for the public plan. Similar evidence of less than 100 percent coverage has been reported by studies of the Massachusetts health reform in 2006, which includes a mandate for individuals to obtain insurance coverage. Kolstad and Kowalski (2012) reported that the insurance coverage level increased to 93.8 percent three years after the reform in Massachusetts.

Figs. 2 and 3 show the trends of medication use in the previous month. For the proportion of those taking at least one medication in the previous month, a distinct trend break in Quebec starting in 1998 is observed. The trend for number of medications taken in the previous month in Quebec is only slightly different from the rest of Canada, although the level is somewhat lower in Quebec. It is interesting to note that Quebec non-elderly residents use medications less often and use fewer types of medications, compared to residents in the rest of Canada. However, data from other sources (e.g., Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), 2011; IMS Health, 2011) report that Quebec residents fill more prescriptions and spend more on prescriptions than residents in the rest of Canada.14 As mentioned, our utilization measure, the number of distinct medications taken, refers to both prescription and nonprescription drugs. It is highly correlated with, but not the same as the number of prescriptions and/or prescription drugs. It is possible that the Quebec residents use more prescriptions but fewer non-prescription drugs.

We use aggregate level expenditure data from CIHI to further look at this issue. We should note that expenditure is not the same as utilization and the data are for all age groups, not just the non-elderly population. Fig. 4 shows total drug expenditure on a per capita basis in Quebec versus the rest of Canada. Before the introduction of the mandatory drug program in 1997, total drug expenditure per capita in Quebec is comparable to that of the rest of Canada; it is higher in Quebec after 1997 (The NPHS data start only part way through the CIHI series depicted in Figs. 4–6). Given that more brand name prescriptions are dispensed in Quebec than the other provinces (IMS Health, 2011), it is possible that the price level for prescription drugs is generally higher in Quebec. Therefore, it is likely that non-elderly Quebec residents use fewer medications than their counterparts in the rest of Canada during our study period 1994 to 2003. Therefore, total drug utilization in Quebec and the rest of Canada from our data is largely consistent with that from the CIHI data.

5. Empirical strategy

We use a difference-in-differences (DD) approach to compare outcomes in Quebec versus other Canadian provinces. The pre-policy period includes the 1994/1995 and 1996/1997 cycles of the NPHS data and the post-policy period includes the three cycles from 1998/1999 to 2002/2003. The treatment group is the general population in Quebec before and after the policy change and the comparison group is the general population in the other provinces of Canada. We employ the following equation to estimate the impact of the reform on insurance coverage, health care utilization and health outcomes:

where $y$ is an outcome variable for individual i in province $p$ at time t, QB is a dummy variable that takes the value of one for individual i in Quebec and zero for the other provinces, and Post takes the value of one for the years after 1997 and zero otherwise. The coefficient, $\beta$ , on the interaction term $( \mathrm { P o s t } ^ { * } Q B )$ gives the impact of the reform, i.e., the change in the outcome before and after the reform in Quebec relative to the other provinces after allowing for the same trend. Province and year dummies are included to control for province and year effects. Other independent variables $( X _ { i p t } )$ include age, sex, marital status, income, education and month of the interview in each survey cycle. In most of the specifications, individual fixed effects are added to control for unobserved individual heterogeneity to identify the policy effect using only the “withinindividual variation”. Detailed descriptions of the independent and dependent variables are shown in Appendix A.

The key identifying assumption in the DD analysis is that the trends in the outcomes of Quebec and the other provinces would have been the same in the absence of the reform. In particular, we assume that the trends in all of the outcomes between Quebec and the other provinces would have been the same in the absence of the reform. There are several reasons to believe that the common trend assumption holds in our analysis. First, as we have mentioned in the institutional setting part, there are minimal drug insurance policy changes among the non-elderly population in the other provinces during our study period. Introduction of the Fair PharmaCare program in British Columbia in 2003 is at the very end of our study period. Second, the institutional context of physician and hospital services is similar across provinces within Canada. All provinces and territories provide universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services that are free at the point of use. Most hospitals are private, not-for-profit organizations funded through global budget. Although there is the introduction and subsequent removal of physician global budgets across a number of the provinces during our study period, these payment changes reforms would likely have reduced use of physician services and biased our estimates downward. The majority of physicians are remunerated by fee for service during our study period 1994 to 2003. Our study period is prior to the primary care reforms in Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec. Actually, there has been little changes in the primary care sector at the system level until the early 2000s (Hutchison et al., 2011). Real transformative changes in the Ontario primary care sector actually happened around the mid 2000s. Third, graphical evidence in the figures show similar trends in the outcomes in Quebec and the rest of Canada. Similarities in summary statistics in Table II suggest that the other provinces serve as a good comparison group. Falsification tests and various model specifications will be conducted to test the identifying assumption and check the robustness of our estimates.

Pooled Poisson models and Poisson models with individualspecific effects are specified for the medication and physician utilization variables since they are count variables.17 Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and/or fixed effects linear probability models are employed for all indicator variables and the HUI measure.18 Using fixed effects models provides an extra advantage of controlling for unobserved time-invariant individual effects. 6.1. Difference-in-differences estimation results

Comparing the four columns, the point estimates of the policy effects do not change notably when control variables are added to the specifications, or when we use a fixed effects rather than an OLS specification. The estimate of the impact on drug utilization is in the middle range of those found in the Medicare Part D studies which vary from 5.9 percent (Yin et al., 2008) to 27 percent (Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010). Given that the utilization measure is total drug utilization, the elasticity for prescription drug utilization would be larger if there is substitution for non-prescription drugs because of the policy intervention. The estimated effects on GP visits are large relative to zero or small spillover effects found in the U.S. context (Balkrishnan et al., 2001; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). This should not be unexpected given that physician services are free in the Canadian context while the multi-payer system in the U.S. varies in co-payment for physician visits across insurance plans.

Panel B of Table IV reports the linear probability regression results for all indicator variables of utilization.22 In both the OLS and fixed effects linear models, coefficient estimates of the policy effects are still very similar in the base model and the model with individual control variables. The mandatory drug program led to an increase in the probability of any medication use in the previous month by 2.2 to 3.2 percentage points. The likelihood of visiting a GP increased by about 2 percentage points although not statistically significant in the fixed effects models. There was little effect on the likelihood of visiting a specialist. Finally both OLS and fixed effects models failed to reveal any statistically significant effects on the likelihood of having an inpatient admission in the previous year.

Panel C of Table IV presents the estimated impact of the mandatory drug program on health status. The program had a small positive effect on self-assessed health status and HUI. Previous studies document that an increase of 0.03 or greater in HUI score is considered as clinically important, and an increase of 0.01 is generally important (Horsman et al., 2003; Grootendorst et al., 2000). The estimated impact on HUI is around 0.010, representing an important improvement in health status.

Our preferred specification is fixed effects Poisson and fixed effects linear models which provide more conservative estimates than those without fixed effects. Therefore, we will focus on the fixed effects Poisson and fixed effects linear models in what follows.

The graphical evidence in Figs. 2, 3, 7 and 8 indicates that the large policy impacts lagged one period relative to the immediate increase in drug coverage after the policy.23 There are some possible explanations to this. First, it takes time for people to adapt to the new policy. Moreover, eligible Quebec residents are required to register for the public plan before it takes effects. Second, physicians, pharmacists and, especially, private insurance companies, also need time to adjust. The physician shortage situation in Quebec in the 1990s also likely made the adjustment slower. We explore the dynamic effects of the policy change in Appendix B and find that the impacts on most of the outcome variables grow larger over time. Overall, the results suggest substantially larger adjustments in drug consumption and GP utilization in the long than short term.

We have shown a reduced form impact of the policy on utilization and health outcomes. If we assume that the policy only affected the reduced form outcomes through the expansion of drug insurance coverage, we can estimate the impact of drug insurance coverage on the outcomes. (The assumption can be violated sometimes; for example, if the contents of the coverage are also changed). Combining the results in Tables III and IV, a one percentage point increase in drug insurance coverage increased medication use in the past month by 0.6 (13/21) percent and annual GP visits by 0.5 (10/21) percent in the population. For the extensive margin, a one percentage point increase in drug insurance coverage increased the probability of any medication use in the previous month by 0.10 (2.2/21) to 0.15 (3.2/21) percentage points in the population. A one percentage point increase in drug insurance coverage increased HUI by 0.0003 in the population. Given that the insurance coverage in the other provinces is 64 percent, we will expect a 22 percent increase in medication use and 18 percent increase in GP visits if all of the other provinces intend to introduce a similar drug plan to cover the 36 percent uninsured.

6.2. Heterogeneous effects at different points of the HUI distribution

DD conditional quantile regression estimates by deciles of HUI are plotted in Fig. 9. We find that the impact on health is monotonically decreasing and is virtually zero from the median to the ninth decile. This finding should not be surprising given that more than 50 percent of the population in the sample have HUI greater than 0.97. It should be noted that the positive impact on HUI is 0.038 at the first decile, representing a clinically important improvement in health status. At the 20th and 30th percentiles, the policy effects are around 0.015 and 0.014 and still statistically significant. These results suggest that it is mainly less healthy individuals that experienced an improvement in health status, indicating that high value pharmaceutical drugs may be under-used among them. Therefore, offering affordable pharmaceutical drugs to these high risk people can improve their health substantially. For policy purposes, this finding is crucial since a mandatory drug program can generate substantial health gains for those with worse health outcomes, who are usually the target of public drug programs. It provides useful information for policymakers who are considering a national pharmacare program in the Canadian context and for optimal drug insurance design in general.
6.3. Subgroup analysis by drug insurance status and chronic condition

One important consideration in understanding the potential effects of the universal drug policy is how it may differentially affect sub-populations. If patients in different subgroups tend to use different combinations of inputs, such as medications, physician and hospital services, to produce health and if health care is more effective for some patients than others, then the benefits of health insurance should vary accordingly. Thanks to the panel nature of the data, individuals who were previously uninsured can be identified and subgroup analysis by previous insurance status is conducted to further identify the heterogeneous impacts of the policy. Similarly, policy effects by chronic condition are estimated. We examine the heterogeneous effects by looking at the interactions between these subgroups and the main treatment variable.

Panel A presents results of drug and physician utilization, Panel B results of the probability of any medication use, a physician visit and hospitalization, and Panel C results of health status. In Panel A, we continue to find evidence of positive policy effects on medication use and GP visits. The effects on medication use are slightly larger for the previously uninsured, but the differences are not statistically significant. The differential effects on GP utilization for the previously insured and uninsured are also not statistically different from zero. We also find large positive effects on specialist visits, with the effects much larger for the previously uninsured, however, none of the estimates are statistically significant. In Panel B, the coefficients of the pre-policy insurance status interactions suggest that the positive effects on the probability of taking medications or visiting a GP are larger for the previously uninsured. We find no evidence of policy effects on the probability of specialist visit and hospitalization. As is shown in column 1 of Panel C, the coefficient on the interaction term suggests that the policy impact on the HUI for the previously uninsured is much smaller than the previously insured. Results in column 2 of Panel C reveal that the previously uninsured are more likely to report excellent or very good health after the policy change but the estimates are not statistically significant.

It is surprising that the results in Table V seem to show that the policy had a large drug utilization impact for the previously insured. However, there are several possible explanations for this. First, this policy required private insurers to have the same level of coverage standard (i.e., drug formulary) as the public plan. Private plans could be more generous than the public plan but not less. Some of the previously insured may increase their utilization as their coverage became more generous. Second, a new public program can stimulate demand on all fronts. It may make people, the previously insured in particular, aware of their drug coverage and ask their doctors to prescribe more for them (Commissaire à La Santé et au Bien-Être, 2015). Finally, the introduction of a large public drug plan may change the market structure of the private drug insurance industry. For example, some evidence suggests that the introduction of Medicare Part D plans led to a large reduction in prices for brand-name prescription drugs with close substitutes (Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010). If this is the case with the Quebec drug insurance market, the previously insured may possibly increase their utilization. Accordingly, the effects on GP utilization are also large among the previously insured because of the complementary relationship between medication use and GP visits.

We further examine the impacts of the policy at different points of the utilization distribution among the previously uninsured and insured. We estimated fixed effects linear probability models (similar to those in columns 1 and 2 in Panel B of Table V), where the dependent variable is an indicator of individuals exceeding specific medication use or physician visit cutoffs (e.g., indicators of using more than two medications, more than three medications etc.). We find that the increase in drug utilization for the previously insured is concentrated at the intensive margin, in contrast to the previously uninsured. Accordingly GP utilization for the previously insured is concentrated at the high end of the distribution, in contrast to the previously uninsured at the low end of the distribution. This seems to imply that there are some changes in the private plan coverage or awareness of it.

6.4. Sensitivity and robustness analysis

We can test the identifying assumption of our DD estimation by falsification (placebo) tests for the years before the policy change. We define 1994/1995 as the pre-policy years and 1996/1997 as the post-policy year in the falsification tests. The test results (shown in Table VII) suggest that none of the coefficients is statistically significant except the coefficient in one of the specialist utilization models, which is significantly negative. Of course, out of 18 coefficient estimates (even if the variables were random numbers) it would be unusual not to have at least one that is statistically significant at the five or ten percent levels. Overall, the falsification tests do not reject the common trend hypothesis in our models. We further estimated full dynamic models by adding all interactions of Quebec and time dummies.25 The results are shown in Appendix B. We find that all coefficients on the interaction of Quebec and year 1994 (two periods before the policy change) are close to zero. Again this indicates that other provinces exhibited a parallel trend to Quebec in all of the outcomes. (Please refer to Appendix B for details).

A number of recent papers have raised concerns about inference in DD estimation (Bertrand et al., 2004; Donald and Lang, 2007; Cameron et al., 2008). The main problem is that the standard errors computed by conventional estimation methods are too small if the error term in the estimating equation includes unobserved groupyear effects (Especially, the errors are serially correlated within groups, leading to inflated t-statistics if this is ignored). To address this serial correlation issue, we compare the standard errors clustered at the province level and individual level. We find that in most cases the standard errors are larger when clustered at the individual level, therefore, we report our main results with standard errors clustered at the individual level. For the Poisson models with individual-specific effects, we report the bootstrapped standard errors.

Several other specifications were estimated to check the robustness of our estimates. As described in Appendix A, all the medication and physician utilization variables are truncated at the 99.5 percentiles. We tried the original values without truncation and the estimates are larger and more significant than those in Table IV. The results are essentially unchanged when we truncate them at the 99th percentiles. Further, including health status, such as self-assessed health status or chronic condition status, as control variables in the utilization equations does not change the estimates substantially. Controlling for initial health status in the first cycle of the survey also makes little difference to our estimates. It may be possible that access to specialists is different from access to GPs, who act as gatekeepers in the health care system, so we included an indicator variable for whether the respondent has a regular family doctor or not in the specialist visit equation. However, there is no meaningful difference in the estimates.
7. Conclusion and discussion

Canada continues to debate the merits of introducing a national pharmacare program. The debate needs to be informed by evidence regarding the effectiveness of expanded drug insurance coverage. This study examines the impact of Quebec’s mandatory universal drug program on insurance coverage, health care utilization and health outcomes. We find that the introduction of the mandatory drug program substantially increased drug coverage among the general population. The program also increased medication use and GP visits. No statistically significant effects were found for specialist visits and hospitalization. Our subgroup analysis by pre-reform drug insurance status suggests that the reform had no differential impacts on total drug and GP utilization among the previously insured and uninsured. Furthermore, effects on drug and GP utilization for the previously uninsured are concentrated at the extensive margin, indicating that the reform improved access to these services for them. Subgroup analysis by presence of chronic condition reveals that the reform had a much large effect on the probability of GP visit for those with chronic conditions. Most importantly, results of quantile regressions show that the reform had differential health impacts. People with worse health outcomes experienced a large improvement in their health status.

Our findings are consistent with most previous studies showing that individuals increase medication use if they have drug insurance. Our estimates of the policy impacts on drug insurance coverage and drug utilization are comparable to those from the existing Medicare Part D studies. This should not be unexpected because the Quebec program and Part D share many similarities. Our finding of a strong positive spillover effect on physician visits is consistent with some previous studies (e.g., Winkelmann, 2004) but in contrast to some Medicare Part D studies reporting zero or small positive spillover effects in the U.S. context (Balkrishnan et al., 2001; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). This implies that the magnitudes of the spillover effects may depend on the institutional context for physician service financing. Our finding of heterogeneous health impacts at different parts of the health distribution provides useful information to understand the link between drug insurance and health status. Previous evidence of no or positive health effects of drug coverage is possibly due to the differences in the health status of the study population.

The findings provide useful information for the implementation of a universal pharmacare program in a public health system. A public drug program covering those who do not have private drug plans can improve access to medications, increase GP visits, and generate substantial health gains for the chronically ill and less healthy people. In the long run, this may lead to reduction in overall health care utilization. The mixed public and private program provides a feasible solution to the design of a national pharmacare program. Given public concerns about the cost of a pure public drug program and the status quo of private insurance industries, the incremental change of adding a public drug plan on top of the private plans is promising. The positive spillover effects on physician visits, which are free in Canada, can also shed light on the policy concern that private drug insurance contributes to the pro-rich inequity in physician utilization (Allin and Hurley, 2009). Offering drug insurance coverage to the low income people, who are less likely to have private drug insurance, may help to reduce such pro-rich inequity.

Future research can build on this study in several ways. For example, we have examined the impact of the drug program on health care utilization and health outcomes; future research can explore the impact on out-of-pocket drug expenditure and total drug expenditure. In addition, if there are data for prescription and non-prescription drug utilization, the policy impact on the substitution between them is another interesting research question.
